findings.title: `cf config unset --project` cannot clear a stale shared-file copy under the design's own delete routing
findings.description: Data Flow states "Delete: mirrors write — deletes from whichever project file the key's scope maps to" (line 89), so after this slice `ConfigManager.delete(key, 'project')` for `git.integration_branch` (a personal key) targets only `.context-forge.local.toml`. But the Collision semantics (line 146) and Verification Walkthrough step 9 (line 259) both instruct the user to clear a stale personal key from the **shared** file via `cf config unset git.integration_branch --project` after `migrate-personal` reports `skipped (personal value already set)`. Under the specified routing that command deletes the developer's local preference from the personal file — the exact value the collision rule protects — and leaves the stale committed copy in `.context-forge.toml`, with `cf check` still warning. The design's stated cleanup path is self-contradictory and silently destructive. The design should either (a) define delete as falling through both project files (remove from personal, then from shared if present there), or (b) give `migrate-personal`/`unset` an explicit, documented way to target the shared file for this one case, and fix verification step 9 to match.

findings.title: Classification table uses a wildcard row that conflicts with the compile-enforced completeness claim
findings.description: The table classifies `workflow.review_gates.*.threshold`, but the actual registry (`packages/core/src/config/ConfigKeys.ts`) has no wildcard key — it declares four explicit keys: `workflow.review_gates.code.threshold`, `workflow.review_gates.arch.threshold`, `workflow.review_gates.slice.threshold`, and `workflow.review_gates.tasks.threshold`. Since the design makes `scope` a required field on `ConfigKeyDefinition` and its Technical Requirements include a "scope classification completeness (every key has a `scope`)" test, the classification table should enumerate the keys that must compile. Expand the wildcard row to the four concrete keys (all clearly `shared`, so the intent carries over) so the table is implementable as written.

findings.title: New `cf check` rule's placement relative to ConsistencyChecker's active-slice gate is unspecified
findings.description: `ConsistencyChecker.check()` returns an empty result when the project has no `fileSlice` (it early-returns on `sliceIndex === null`), while `checkAll()` runs the aggregate/document-wide rules regardless. The Verification Walkthrough's scratch project is `cf init --lite` in an empty directory — no active slice — so steps 5 and 7 ("Run cf check … confirm a warning-severity finding") will only pass if the new `personal-config-in-shared-file` rule runs on the `checkAll` path (or if `cf check` resolves a slice). The design should state which method hosts the rule, matching how `ruleFrontmatterSchema` is a `checkAll`-only rule.

findings.title: "reusing the pattern already used for personal ignores" is not accurate
findings.description: Technical Scope says the gitignore change "reuses the pattern already used for personal ignores", but there is no existing personal-ignore pattern in the codebase (confirmed: no gitignore logic in `packages/cli` or `packages/core`, which the design itself restates at line 159). The later section describes the actual behavior (create or append one line) correctly; this line just overstates reuse. Harmless, but trimming it avoids an implementer hunting for a nonexistent pattern.

findings.title: Collision "identical values" case reported as "moved" although nothing moves
findings.description: When a personal key exists identically in both files, the design deletes the shared copy but says to "report it as moved" — nothing was written to the personal file, so a `moved` report mislabels a delete-only operation and would confuse the walkthrough's expectations (step 9's report shape). Consider a distinct label (e.g. `cleaned redundant shared copy`) or at least note the wording is illustrative.
